title: Weekly Top Five Articles: Confessions of an Overthinker
author: Anthony B. Bradley
summary: Anthony Bradley departs from his usual wide-ranging weekly roundup to confess that he is a chronic overthinker whose anxiety sometimes costs him sleep and appetite. He organizes five readings around overthinking, catastrophizing, and anxiety, adding his own interpretive commentary to each. The selections run from Donald Robertson on the Stoic sage who still feels fear but copes wisely, to a counseling blog on the hunt for certainty, Roger McFillin on a picture book that teaches children to fear their own nerves, Christian Poensgen on how beliefs about stress shape its effects, and Jack Nollan on cognitive traps. Across the commentary Bradley draws out a common thread: wisdom lies in how we carry involuntary emotion and in what we train our attention to see. He closes by admitting that he regularly teaches these techniques yet struggles to practice them himself.
points: Bradley frames the roundup as personal, reading these pieces for himself during a bout of debilitating overthinking.
From Robertson he highlights that the Stoic sage still feels the first movements of fear, and wisdom shows in how they are carried.
He endorses McFillin's warning that teaching children every flutter needs treatment teaches them to fear fear itself.
Poensgen's research summary suggests that stress raised mortality risk only among people who believed stress was harmful.
Nollan's piece supports his conclusion that attention is a practice and that we come to see what we repeatedly focus on.
quotes: I have a confession: I’m a chronic, neurotic overthinker. It’s really, really bad. If Paul was the “chief of sinners,” I am the “chief of worriers.

I’m departing from my normal wide range of weekly articles to focus on overthinking, catastrophizing, negative filtering, anxiety, hypervigilance, and so on, mainly because I’m reading these right now.
The big interpretive point is that the Stoic Sage experienced the propatheiai—the involuntary first movements of fear or distress—but wisdom is shown in how you carry them.
When a child is taught that every flutter must be medicated, she learns to fear fear itself.
It’s significant because how we interpret that physiological response can be lethal:
The interpretive revelation is that attention is a practice. What we repeatedly focus on becomes what we are capable of seeing.

I tell other people about prayer and casting one’s burdens on the Lord. I even mention many of the techniques discussed in the articles above, but when it comes to my own circumstances, I am a terrible practitioner.
